title: OpenAI Bans Russian and Iranian Networks Using ChatGPT for Influence Campaigns
excerpt: The company says the Russian 'Dark Clark' operation was the most sophisticated front-identity campaign it has disrupted, while Iran's 'Bogus Bylines' placed nearly 100 articles in real outlets under fake journalist personas.
body:
• OpenAI said Thursday it banned clusters of ChatGPT accounts in Russia and Iran that were using its tools to run covert influence operations built around "false front" entities.
  • The Russian "Dark Clark" operation is the first Category 5 case OpenAI has disrupted — it targeted Latin America with fake narratives, fabricated media and a bogus think tank.
  • Iran's "Bogus Bylines" ran seven fake journalist personas that placed nearly 100 articles in about a dozen real outlets, including Daily Kos and the Middle East Monitor.
  • Why it matters: operatives claimed planted narratives were picked up by real media and even drew a response from a European lawmaker. Check viral claims against established outlets before sharing.

OpenAI said Thursday it had banned networks of ChatGPT accounts in Russia and Iran that were using its artificial intelligence tools to power covert influence campaigns across multiple countries — the latest and most ambitious operations of their kind the company says it has found.

The company disclosed the takedowns in a safety report published October 8, saying both operations used "false front" entities — fake think tanks, fake journalists, fabricated documents — to, in its words, "launder geopolitical, conflict-related messaging into their target audiences."

"Dark Clark": Russia's Latin America campaign

OpenAI assessed the Russian operation at Category 5 on the IO Breakout Scale, the industry standard for rating influence operations from 1 (lowest) to 6 (highest).

https://youtube.com/watch?v=8o8kmkaiYF4

According to OpenAI's report, the operators — who mostly prompted in Russian and used VPNs to circumvent the company's ban on access from Russia — used ChatGPT chiefly to draft internal reports to an unknown superior. The reports covered three workstreams: denigrating Ukraine and undermining recruitment for the Ukrainian armed forces; interfering in domestic politics, particularly in Bolivia and Argentina; and running a self-styled research platform called the Social Research Center, controlled through a fake persona named "Mia Clark."

The internal reports claimed a string of planted fakes: a false 2024 story that Argentine President Javier Milei had bought jeweled collars for his dogs; and in May 2026, an impersonation of the Regional Directorate of Education in Lima that got Peruvian schools to hold Ukraine-themed events referencing Stepan Bandera, the controversial Ukrainian nationalist. Peruvian outlet Extra confirmed one such school event took place, and a Polish news report about it prompted a far-right Polish member of the European Parliament to suggest banning entry to Bandera supporters. OpenAI said its research found matching media coverage and official debunks for several more claimed fakes in Ecuador and Bolivia.

Notably, the Social Research Center's website describes a focus on the Indian diaspora in Latin America, and OpenAI said the evidence indicated the platform's on-the-ground employees were unaware they were working for a Russian group. The company identified more than 60 articles on the site, mostly apparently original compositions.

"Bogus Bylines": Iran's fake journalists

The Iranian operation ran seven fake journalist personas that pitched and polished long-form articles for small and medium-sized online outlets around the world. OpenAI identified nearly 100 articles published or syndicated under the operation's bylines across roughly a dozen outlets focused on international affairs and the Middle East, running from July 2025 through October 2026, with frequency increasing after the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran conflict.

The fake authors landed articles in outlets including the progressive U.S. news site Daily Kos and the U.K.-based Middle East Monitor. According to NBC News, the Middle East Monitor published at least 21 articles by four of the fake authors before taking down their author pages. Alongside the articles, the operators generated batches of social-media comments portraying the United States as the aggressor, Israel as an unreliable ally and Iran as a resilient victim. OpenAI said the campaign appeared consistent with a commercial actor running a for-hire influence operation, though it could not identify who that was.

"AI was valuable to them above and beyond just being a shortcut… It helped them create language that looked and felt and read authentic to the point where it was being published by legitimate outlets."

— a researcher quoted by NPR

Why media placement matters

OpenAI said it has now exposed 30 covert influence operations over the past two and a half years, and found that campaigns that land their content in real media outlets reach far wider audiences than those relying on fake social-media accounts alone.

What to watch

The findings underscore a shift: the cutting edge of influence operations is no longer fake social-media accounts, but content polished enough to pass an editor's desk. OpenAI's safety report warned that operations breaking into established media have the highest potential reach of any campaign type.

For NRIs, the report carries a direct warning: one of the Russian fronts posed as a platform covering the Indian diaspora in Latin America — evidence that diaspora communities are valuable targets for influence operations. When a dramatic claim about Ukraine, elections or India circulates online, check whether an established outlet with named reporters has independently confirmed it before sharing.
